title: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?
summary:
Major tours by the likes of Oasis helped make 2025 a lucrative year, with music export revenue reaching £4.8bn

Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by…

blocks.text: Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by the likes of Olivia Dean, have helped to push the UK music industry to record revenues.
But there are concerns over a widening gulf in income between A-listers such as these, and the less well-known artists that form the bulk of the UK’s music community.

The annual report by UK Music, an umbrella organisation featuring various industry bodies, finds that music added £8.4bn to the UK economy in 2025, a record figure and an inflation-outpacing rise of 5.7% from the previous year.

Export revenue rose 3.6%, to £4.8bn, encompassing money made outside the UK by British artists – including via international touring and royalties and revenues raised from sales and streaming of music abroad.
There was also a slight rise in employment in the sector in the UK: 730 jobs were added, to take total recorded employment to 220,500.

The success is powered in part by a live music sector in which stadium performances – once the preserve of only the very top artists – are becoming increasingly commonplace, with consumers willing to spend three-figure sums on tickets.

However, the This Is Music report cautioned that “many emerging and grassroots artists experienced rising costs which reduced net incomes, and even well-known artists have found it hard to make money”.

The report highlights a number of hit albums by UK artists that have helped boost recorded music revenues – including No 1s by Sleep Token, Yungblud, Sam Fender, Wet Leg, and Biffy Clyro – but also highlighted a troubling trend.

blocks.caption: British metal band Sleep Token, who scored a No 1 album in 2025. Photograph: Helle Arensbak/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In terms of album consumption figures, UK artists had historically been more popular than US ones in the domestic marketplace, but US artists overtook UK ones in 2018 and their popularity has continued to diverge, levelling out somewhat in 2025 thanks in part to blockbuster hits by Dean, Fender and others.

AI also threatens to divert listeners’ attention away from human artists, with the report warning: “AI generated ‘slop’ and deepfakes are an increasing problem, which is reflected in a dramatic increase in takedown notices for AI deepfakes issued by labels,” referring to songs taken down from streaming services for imitating existing artists.

There was a marked difference between two sets of data the study used to monitor the income of artists. A survey of the accounts for “top and mid-level” artists found that these musicians were flush, their earnings rising more than 14% year on year. But the Music Creators’ Survey, which asks musicians (including artists, songwriters, producers, composers and more) to self-report their income, found growth of just 0.2% in the same period.

“It has never been easier to record and release music, but given the intense level of competition that has ensued, it has never been more difficult to establish a profile and build a scalable career,” reads the report. “This makes life especially tough for many music creators with average earnings.

“Once artists and music creators break through beyond a certain level, more options and better terms of business can enhance their careers very significantly, but the challenge remains developing more artists and creators to that level.”

UK Music is made up of industry bodies, including royalty agencies PRS for Music and PPL; the BPI, the collective body for the UK’s record labels; AIM, which represents the independent label sector; plus the Musicians’ Union and more.

Tom Kiehl, UK Music’s chief executive, used the report’s launch to lobby the government on a range of issues. “The government must use the upcoming UK EU summit on 20 November to work to remove barriers to EU exports,” he said. “It must not give AI a free pass and should support a sustainably funded BBC – and deliver economic growth for music in every postcode.

He added: “We are not simply asking government to act. We stand ready to be part of the solution too. The UK music industry has never lacked talent, ambition or creativity. The challenge now is ensuring the right environment exists for those strengths to flourish. If we get that right, the opportunities ahead are enormous.”

Ian Murray, creative industries minister, highlighted government funding schemes such as the Music Growth Package and said: “We are investing in the grassroots infrastructure, talent pipeline and independent businesses that keep the sector competitive.”
Some of the UK’s most successful acts are already eyeing a potentially lucrative 2027.

Oasis will head back out on tour after the blockbuster success of their 2025 reunion, playing 11 different locations across the UK, Europe and North America; Dua Lipa has been announced as a headliner of Coachella festival and is expected to release a fourth studio album; and Sam Fender has announced the Proper Massive tour, with 12 UK and Ireland stadium dates plus major venues in North America.
